chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from al-Qasim ibn Sulayman, from Ubayd ibn Zurara, from his father, from a man who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'Supplication — it is the worship about which God (Mighty and Majestic) said: "Indeed those who are too proud to worship Me" — the verse [40:60]. Supplicate to God (Mighty and Majestic) and do not say that the matter has already been decided.'
Zurara said: 'What he means is: your faith in the divine decree and pre-determination should not prevent you from being diligent in supplication and striving in it — or words to that effect.'

key_terms.الاستكبار: Arrogance/pride (istikbar); specifically refusing to humble oneself by calling upon God.
key_terms.الدعاء: Du'a — supplication; calling upon God directly. In this hadith, it is identified as the core meaning of worship ('ibada).
key_terms.العبادة: Worship ('ibada); here specifically referring to the act of du'a as the purest form of worship.
key_terms.القضاء والقدر: Qada' and Qadar — divine decree and pre-determination. The theological doctrine that all events are ordained by God.

ai.seo_question: Is supplication (du'a) the essence of worship in Islam?
ai.summary: Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) identifies supplication (du'a) as the very essence of worship, citing Quran 40:60 where God rebukes those who are too proud to call upon Him. The Imam instructs believers to keep supplicating and warns against using the doctrine of divine decree (qada' and qadar) as an excuse to abandon du'a. The narrator Zurara adds an important theological clarification: belief in predetermination is not meant to make one passive, but rather should coexist with active and diligent supplication — a key balance in Shia theology between divine will and human agency.
